extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when statements by an applicant or claim drafting constitute admissions that may be used as prior art for anticipation or obviousness, and how examiners should treat such admissions during examination. Covers specification statements, Jepson claims, and the effect (or lack thereof) of listing references in an IDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant constitute prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as prior art under the statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., 324 F.3d 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2003); Constant v. Advanced Micro-Devices Inc., 848 F.2d 1560 (Fed. Cir. 1988). If the admitted prior art anticipates the claim but does not qualify as prior art under any paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102, the claim may nevertheless be rejected as anticipated by the admitted prior art without citing 35 U.S.C. 102. (Also note caveat regarding same inventive entity—see separate metric.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Work of the same inventive entity labeled 'prior art' is not automatically prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if labeled as 'prior art,' the work of the same inventive entity may not be considered prior art against the claims unless it falls under one of the statutory categories of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Reading & Bates Construction Co. v. Baker Energy Resources Corp., 748 F.2d 645 (Fed. Cir. 1984). The principle is that an inventor's own earlier work should not, without a statutory basis, be treated as prior art solely because the inventor admits knowledge of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must determine whether an 'admission' is another's work or the inventor's own
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant identifies subject matter as 'prior art,' the examiner must determine whether that subject matter is the inventor's own work or the work of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In making this determination, the examiner should consider any credible explanation provided by the applicant; in the absence of another credible explanation, examiners should treat the subject matter as the work of another. This determines whether the admission can be used as prior art against the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion of prior art in the specification constitutes an admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification identifies work done by another as 'prior art,' the subject matter so identified is treated as admitted prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Nomiya, 509 F.2d 566 (CCPA 1975) — applicant’s labeling of figures as 'prior art' was held to be an admission that the pictured material was prior art relative to the claimed improvement. Examiners should treat explicit identification in the specification as an admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-format claims imply admission that the preamble is prior art (with possible rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR 1.75(e); MPEP §608.01(m); In re Fout, 675 F.2d 297 (CCPA 1982). This implication may be overcome if the applicant gives another credible reason for using Jepson format (see In re Ehrreich, 590 F.2d 902 (CCPA 1979), where use to avoid double patenting was an acceptable explanation). Also, if the Jepson preamble actually describes the inventor’s own work, it should not be used against the claims (see Reading & Bates; Ehrreich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing a reference in an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is not an admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere listing of a reference in an IDS is not taken as an admission that the reference is prior art against the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., 324 F.3d 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2003); 37 CFR 1.97(h) ("The filing of an information disclosure statement shall not be construed to be an admission that the information cited in the statement is, or is considered to be, material to patentability..."). Listing an inventor's own prior patent in an IDS does not make it available as prior art absent a statutory basis.
